nameStory: The toad lily gets its quirky name from its spotted flowers, which reminded someone of the warty, speckled skin of a toad. The scientific name 'hirta' means 'hairy,' referring to the fuzzy texture you'll feel when you touch the leaves and stems.
description: Toad lily is an unusual perennial that brings an exotic touch to New England gardens, though it's rarely seen in the wild here. This Japanese native grows 2-3 feet tall with large, clasping leaves that wrap around upright stems. In late summer and fall, it produces distinctive orchid-like flowers that are white to pale purple with dark purple spots, creating an almost tropical appearance in temperate gardens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six-petaled flowers are white to pale purple with striking dark purple spots, resembling tiny orchids. They appear in clusters along the upper stems and have a waxy texture with prominent stamens.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, oval leaves clasp directly around the stem without stalks, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch. They're arranged alternately up the stem and have parallel veins typical of lilies.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps of upright, unbranched stems that arch gracefully as they mature. The whole plant has a soft, herbaceous feel and dies back completely in winter.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Both stems and leaves feel noticeably hairy or fuzzy when you run your fingers over them, giving the plant a soft, velvety texture throughout.

habitat: In New England, toad lily is primarily found in cultivated gardens rather than wild settings. When it does naturalize, look for it in moist, shaded areas with rich soil, similar to its native habitat on rocky cliffs and stream banks in Japan. It prefers woodland edges and shaded slopes with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge late in spring, unfurling soft, fuzzy leaves that clasp around sturdy stems. Plants grow slowly at first, building up their leafy structure.
seasonality.summer: Foliage reaches full size through summer, creating attractive arching clumps. Flower buds begin forming in late summer but haven't opened yet.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular spotted flowers bloom from late August through October, making this one of the latest-blooming lilies. Peak flowering often coincides with early fall foliage.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to the ground, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Toad lilies are so rare in wild New England that they've been observed only 3 times total, making them one of the rarest lily family members in the region—you're more likely to spot one in a gardener's shade collection than in the woods!
confusionNotes: The spotted flowers might remind you of native trout lilies, but trout lilies bloom in early spring, have only two leaves, and grow from bulbs. Toad lilies bloom in fall, have many stem-clasping leaves, and grow from rhizomes (underground stems).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'lily,' toad lilies are only distantly related to true lilies and don't grow from bulbs like most plants we call lilies. They're primarily garden plants in New England, originally from Japan where they have cultural significance and several poetic names.
compareHints: The only other toad lily you might encounter in New England gardens is Tricyrtis formosana, which has more upright flowers that face outward rather than drooping slightly downward. Formosana also tends to bloom a bit earlier and has less prominently hairy leaves, though both species share that distinctive spotted flower pattern that makes toad lilies unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Japanese Toad Lily (Tricyrtis hirta), the Formosan species is completely hairless and tends to have slightly larger, more boldly spotted flowers.
